title: Bytes on the Wire: What a Struct Is Not

questions.question: Why does sending a struct with reinterpret_cast work between two copies of your own program and fail against a device?
options: Both copies were built by the same compiler, which made the same padding and byte order decisions
The device is slower and drops bytes
reinterpret_cast is only valid within one process
The struct is copied twice on the way out
questions.explanation: The test that would have caught it is the one you did not write, because both ends of your test agreed about everything that was never written down.

questions.question: A struct holds a uint8_t, a double and a uint16_t. Eleven bytes of data. What does sizeof report and why?
options: Twenty four, because the double must sit at an address that is a multiple of eight and the compiler pads to arrange it
Eleven, since sizeof is the sum of the members
Sixteen, always, because structs round up to a power of two
It is unspecified and cannot be measured
questions.explanation: Reordering the fields gives sixteen for the same data. The number is a decision your compiler made for your processor, and the device made a different one.

questions.question: Why write bytes with shifts rather than copying the memory of the value?
options: A shift is arithmetic on a number and means the same thing everywhere, while the memory layout is whatever this processor's byte order is
Shifting is faster
memcpy cannot be used on integers
Shifting avoids undefined behaviour that memcpy would cause
questions.explanation: Code written with shifts has no endianness at all. It produces the bytes the protocol asked for wherever it is compiled, which is the property you want.

questions.question: Why is memcpy the way to get at the bits of a float, rather than casting a pointer?
options: The cast breaks the aliasing rules and can be misaligned, which faults on some ARM cores, and memcpy compiles to the same instruction
memcpy is faster than a cast
A float cannot be pointed at
The cast rounds the value
questions.explanation: The cast usually works, until a release build with optimisation on, which is the worst possible moment to discover it. memcpy costs nothing but knowing to write it.

questions.question: Your decoder round trips every value correctly in tests and still reads garbage from the device. What did the tests not check?
options: The actual bytes, since an encoder and decoder that are both backwards agree with each other perfectly
That the values were large enough
That the buffer was big enough
That the device was connected
questions.explanation: A round trip tests that two halves of your own code agree. Only pinning the bytes tests that they agree with the specification.

questions.question: Why must a buffer be uint8_t rather than char?
options: char is signed on some platforms and unsigned on others, so a byte above 127 reads as a negative number on one and not the other
char is only one byte on some platforms
uint8_t is faster to index
char cannot hold binary data
questions.explanation: The disagreement lives in the type rather than in the logic, so reading the logic will not find it. A checksum over the same bytes gets two different answers.
